name: MATLAB
title: MATLAB (R2026a)

type.text: **Dynamic typing with no static check (T1)**: A variable takes its type from the value assigned to it, so a type error is reported only when the statement runs

**A numeric value carries a class but no shape**: `double` is the default for a literal, and a 1×1 scalar, a vector, and a matrix are the same class, so the type does not state the dimensions the algorithm needs
**Cell arrays and structs are weak structural types**: They group heterogeneous values but declare no schema, so a consumer learns a struct's fields from the code that fills it

**Only a package folder scopes a name**: A `+pkg` folder gives its functions and classes their own namespace, but a plain function or script on the search path shares one flat name space with every other file on the path, so a collision is resolved by path order
**Argument validation is opt-in**: An `arguments` block (R2019b+) checks class, size, and shape at call time, but a function without one accepts anything

construction.text: **Toolboxes separate domain computation from the core language**: Signal Processing, Control System, and Image Processing operations are ordinary function calls, so an algorithm does not embed its own filter or transform code
**A `classdef` file groups state with its operations**: Properties and methods are declared in one unit, so a consumer binds to the class name
**Global mutable state by default (C1)**: The base workspace and every shared function workspace hold variables that running code can read and overwrite at any time
**No immutability by default (C2)**: Every array is mutable, and there is no `const`-like freeze for ordinary data
**Constructors are ordinary methods with no enforced invariant**: A class defines its own `Name(...)` constructor, so a well-formed instance depends on the author's validation
**Scripts run in the caller's workspace**: A variable a script creates stays in the caller after the script returns, so a script couples to every caller's variable names

memory.text: **Copy-on-modify protects the reader**: An assignment copies a value only when the copy is modified, so a function that receives an array does not change the caller's value
**The collector runs on its own schedule (M2)**: Memory returns when the interpreter decides, so release timing is not owned by the code
**No RAII (M3)**: There is no block-scoped destructor, so a file handle, timer, or instrument connection stays open until `delete` or an `onCleanup` object runs
**No ownership model (M4)**: No static lifetime or aliasing rule ties an array's storage to one owner
**`clear` and `pack` are manual controls**: Freeing a large array and defragmenting the workspace are explicit calls, so the memory strategy is the programmer's

error.text: **`try`/`catch` gives a structured recovery path**: A `catch` block receives the `MException` object, with its identifier, message, and stack, so recovery need not parse text
**`error` takes a stable identifier**: `error('pkg:func:reason', ...)` sets `MException.identifier`, so a caller can branch on the code rather than on the message
**Unchecked exceptions only (Er2)**: A raised `MException` travels up until something catches it or the program stops, and no caller is required to handle it
**An empty `catch` is common in legacy code**: A `catch` block with no body discards the failure without a trace
**Many failures are detected only at run time**: An out-of-bound index, a class mismatch, or a singular matrix is reported when the statement executes

concurrency.text: **Manual synchronisation with no race detection (K3)**: `parfor`, `spmd`, and `parfeval` leave the shared-variable reasoning to the programmer, and the language reports no data race
**`parfor` separates loop iterations**: An independent loop is split across workers, so iteration order is not part of the result
**`labSend` and `labReceive` pass data between `spmd` workers**: A worker sends a value to a named peer instead of writing into shared memory
**The parallel constructs need the Parallel Computing Toolbox**: `parfor`, distributed arrays, and `parpool` are a separate licensed product
**A captured variable is broadcast to every worker**: A `parfor` body sees a copy of the outer variable, and a reduction must use a supported form or a temporary variable

platform.text: **GNU Octave is a compatible open implementation**: Most MATLAB programs run under Octave, so a project is not bound to one vendor's binary alone
**A licence still governs the base product**: An installation of MATLAB itself needs a licence, so deployment and continuous integration depend on MathWorks' terms and pricing
**Toolbox coverage is proprietary**: Domain functions come from licensed MathWorks toolboxes, so portability depends on which toolboxes the code calls
**A compiled component still needs the MATLAB Runtime**: MATLAB Compiler builds a library callable from C, C++, .NET, or Python, but the component runs against a version-matched MATLAB Runtime

performance.text: **Matrix expressions call tuned BLAS and LAPACK libraries**: `A*B`, `A\b`, and `fft` run in compiled libraries, so numerical throughput does not depend on hand-written loops
**Vectorisation removes per-element interpreter overhead**: One array expression is one interpreted call, whatever the element count
**The interpreter performs no ahead-of-time compilation (R1)**: Base MATLAB executes an interpreted form, so a loop that cannot be vectorised is slower than its compiled equivalent
**The execution engine compiles eligible code just in time**: The engine introduced in R2015b accelerates a repeated loop after warm-up
**Speed follows the shipped library, not the source**: The cost of a signal-processing or control operation depends on the toolbox build and on the CPU it was tuned for

ecosystem.text: **The ecosystem is proprietary (Ec4)**: Toolboxes, the editor, and the reference documentation come from one vendor under licence
**The toolbox library covers most engineering fields**: Optimization, Statistics and Machine Learning, Signal Processing, and Control System toolboxes are long-established products
**The Add-On Explorer installs packages by name**: MathWorks and community add-ons are installed through one manager, so a project does not have to vendor source
**MATLAB Central File Exchange is a large community index**: User-contributed functions and toolboxes are published together and searchable
**Toolboxes ship in lockstep with the release**: A toolbox is versioned for the MATLAB release it targets, so an upgrade can require every toolbox to move
**Every tool in the chain assumes a licensed installation**: Editors and continuous-integration integrations exist, but they resolve back to a licensed MATLAB

evolution.text: **Backward compatibility is a stated commitment**: MathWorks keeps old syntax working and warns before a feature is removed, so a program from an earlier release generally still runs
**Two releases a year on a known cadence**: R2026a and R2026b follow a predictable schedule, so an upgrade path can be planned
**`verLessThan` lets one source span two releases**: A program can branch on the MATLAB version, so an old and a new release can be supported together
**An upgrade can change performance or a default**: A new execution engine, a new library version, or a changed default can alter timing or output for code that relied on the old behaviour
**A deprecated function may stop working later**: Deprecation is announced, but a function or toolbox marked for removal eventually goes away

domain.text: **Excellent fit for numerical linear algebra**: Matrix syntax, `\` for a linear solve, and N-D arrays match the mathematics directly
**Signal processing, control systems, and image processing are first-class domains**: Each ships as an endorsed toolbox with the reference algorithms
**Domain and vendor lock-in (D1)**: The language and its library set target one vendor's platform, so adoption is also a procurement decision
**Simulink is a second modelling toolchain**: A graphical model is not MATLAB source, so a control design that uses Simulink couples to a second product and file format
**General application work sits outside the design centre**: File handling, text processing, and network code read as additions to a numerical language

learning.text: **Moderate at the start and steeper later (L1)**: `A\b` and `1:n` are learnable in days, while vectorisation, the workspace model, and copy semantics take practice
**The workspace model confuses newcomers**: A variable a script creates persists in the caller, so a beginner cannot tell where state lives
**One-based indexing diverges from most languages**: Code ported from a C-family or Python source needs every index checked by hand
**Documentation is uniform and complete**: Every function has a reference page with examples, and the language is taught in standard textbooks
**Toolbox knowledge is separate from language knowledge**: Finding the right function means knowing which toolbox owns the domain

syntax.text: **Matrix-oriented and compact**: `A(:, 2) = A(:, 1) * 3;` expresses a whole-column operation in one statement
**Keyword-light and readable**: Most statements are operations on data, with few punctuation-only constructs
**Element-wise and matrix operators differ by one dot**: `*` versus `.*` and `^` versus `.^` are distinct operations, so a missing dot silently changes the computation
**`end` is overloaded**: It terminates a block and marks the last index inside a subscript
**The semicolon controls output rather than the statement**: A missing `;` prints every intermediate result, which clutters a long run

testing.text: **A test framework ships in the base product**: `matlab.unittest.TestCase`, `functiontests`, and `runtests` provide assertions, fixtures, and parameterised cases
**A failure reports the value and the assertion**: The framework prints the constraint that failed and the observed value, so a failure is localised
**Mocking and coverage are part of the framework**: `matlab.mock` creates replacement objects, and the code-coverage plugin reports unexecuted lines
**A test suite lives in function files beside the code**: There is no separate test manifest, so a suite's scope follows the folder layout
**Automated runs need a licence**: Continuous integration needs a licence seat or a pre-built component with the MATLAB Runtime

security.text: **No pointers and no manual memory access**: The language offers no address arithmetic, so a buffer overflow cannot be written in MATLAB source
**External access is explicit in the source**: `fopen`, `readmatrix`, and `webread` are visible calls, so a reader can see every file and network access
**`eval`, `evalin`, and `str2func` execute text as code**: A string built from untrusted input can become a statement, which is the injection pattern
**`load` can introduce undeclared variables**: Restoring a `.mat` file creates variables whose names the source does not state, and such a name can shadow a live variable
**Static proof of run-time error freedom needs a separate product**: Polyspace Code Prover proves the absence of certain run-time errors, but it is licensed apart from the language

tradeoffs: **One-based indexing is a convention choice**: Starting an array at index 1 is a documented decision, and the cost is re-learning for a user who comes from a zero-based language
**The global workspace suits interactive work**: A session-wide namespace is convenient at the command line, and the coupling it creates at scale follows from using session state as program state
**Everything-is-an-array is a deliberate uniformity**: One container for scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D arrays keeps the language small, and the loss of shape in the type is the price
**The filename rule is a lookup convention**: A function file is named for its entry point, and local functions in scripts (a later addition) reduce the constraint
**A proprietary platform is traded for an integrated toolchain**: The licence buys one install, one editor, and one support channel
**Scripts are for session-scale tasks**: Converting a script to a function removes the caller-workspace coupling
verdict: MATLAB's design yields moderate language-imposed coupling for numerical engineering work. Matrix operations remove per-element iteration from the source, and toolboxes separate domain algorithms from the core language. Main strengths: an excellent fit for linear algebra, signal processing, and control systems; a large library; and a strong backward-compatibility record. Main weaknesses: the base workspace and every script variable form one shared mutable namespace with no namespaces, typing is dynamic with no static check, indexing is one-based against most languages, and the whole platform is proprietary, so cost and portability follow MathWorks' licence and pricing.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.
